bib.title: From LLMs to LLM-based Agents for Software Engineering: A Survey of Current, Challenges and Future

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "From LLMs to LLM-based Agents for Software Engineering: A Survey of Current, Challenges and Future", Haolin Jin, Linghan Huang, Haipeng Cai, Jun Yan, Bo Li, Huaming Chen. arXiv:2408.02479v2 [cs.SE], dated 13 Apr 2025 in the stamp. It uses a "Journal of LaTeX Class Files" template, so I found no venue and treat it as a preprint. The collection window is "latter half of 2023 and before December 2024".

COVERAGE: 306,435 of 306,435 chars read, which is all 50 PDF pages (printed pp. 1-47 plus reference pages). Tables, the Section X discussion, the challenges list and the conclusion are all in that range. References (about chars 262,000 to the end) were skimmed only. Figures were not rendered; I used the text extracted from their captions.

CLAIMS (most important first)

- The survey admits there is no accepted definition of an LLM-based agent in SE. It proposes six criteria and calls a system an agent if it "meets most".
  - number: 6 criteria. Criteria 1-4 are the basic level of agency. Criteria 5-6 are advanced and "not strictly necessary".
  - setup: criteria synthesised from H1-2024 works (SWE-agent, CodeAgent, AutoCodeRover, GOEX, MetaGPT, AgentVerse, Reflexion, ExpeL). SE-specific.
  - quote: "Currently, there is no comprehensive and widely accepted definition specifying the exact capabilities an LLM must exhibit to be considered an LLM-based agent, particularly within the context of software engineering."
  - quote: "we define an LLM architecture as an agent if it meets most of the criteria listed in Table V. Criteria 1 to 4 (LLM as central reasoning core, decision-making and planning, autonomous tool usage, and evaluation capabilities) are considered fundamental for a basic level of agency. Criteria 5 and 6 (contextual multi-turn interaction and autonomous learning capability) indicate more advanced agentic behaviors"
  - where: Section III-E, pp. 8-9

- Table V, the criteria themselves.
  - number: 6
  - quote: "1) The LLM serves as the brain (the center of information processing and generation of thought)." / "2) The framework not only relies on the language understanding and generation capabilities of LLMs but also possesses decision-making and planning abilities." / "3) If tools are available, the model can autonomously decide when and which tools to use and integrate the results into its predictions" / "4) The model can select the optimal solution from multiple homogeneous results (the ability to evaluate and choose among various possible solutions)." / "5) The model can handle multiple interactions and maintain contextual understanding." / "6) The model has autonomous learning capabilities and adaptability."
  - where: p. 9

- Component framing. The survey does not define an architecture of perception, memory, planning and action. I searched the full text. "Perception" appears only in the places below, and "memory module" and "planning module" never appear.
  - The Fudan survey [10] "examining their perception, behavior, and cognition" (p. 6).
  - ClarifyGPT: "This pipeline, involving perception, planning, action, and reflection, exemplifies typical LLM-based agent characteristics." (p. 18)
  - PCA-EVAL scores: "Perception Score (P-Score), Cognition Score (C-Score), and Action Score (A-Score)" (p. 26).
  - Fig. 8 labels a "Perception Module", an Inspection Agent and a Skill Library in XUAT-Copilot (p. 33).
  - The nearest to an agent definition: "Traditional LLMs typically generate responses based solely on given natural language descriptions, lacking the ability for independent thinking and judgment. LLM-based agents able to employ multiple rounds of interaction and customized prompts to gather more information" (p. 6).
  - Memory appears as explicit memory pools and experience tracking: ExpeL uses "a memory pool and insights pool" (p. 25). Challenge 2 of the future work asks for "Enhancing agent memory and reflection mechanisms" (p. 45).
  - On the LLM as the "brain": "researchers exploring the use of large language models as the 'brain' of AI agents" (p. 6).

- Corpus size and scope.
  - number: 139 papers; six SE domains; 82 unique LLMs used in experiments.
  - setup: DBLP and arXiv search, keyword AND/OR queries, snowballing, manual screening. Excludes papers under 7 pages and grey literature.
  - quote: "we have collected a total of 139 papers directly relevant to this topic" (p. 3)
  - quote: "across the 139 papers, we identified a total of 82 unique large language models" (p. 40)
  - quote: "Specifically, 'the collection primarily focuses on the latter half of 2023 and before December 2024'" (p. 2; the exact text is "Since the collection primarily focuses on the latter half of 2023 and before December 2024")

- Venue mix.
  - number: arXiv 40.3%, so 59.7% peer-reviewed.
  - quote: "The prominence of arXiv (40.3%) reflects the field's rapid evolution... Notably, 59.7% of papers originate from established peer-reviewed venues" (p. 4)

- Topic split of papers. Fig. 12 gives 76 LLM and 77 agent instances (sum 153), because papers can count in several topics.
  - LLM papers: REQ 20, Code 16, Autonomous 6, Design 8, Test 9, Security 17.
  - Agent papers: REQ 6, Code 20, Autonomous 23, Design 9, Test 6, Security 13.
  - quote: "The most prominent theme is autonomous learning and decision making, comprising nearly 30% of all agent-related papers" (p. 42)
  - quote: "the literature review in the figure includes more than 139 total paper instances" (p. 4)
  - Table I task totals: REQ 28, Code 35, Autonomous 30, Design 19, Test 15, Security/Maintenance 43.

- Agents use different benchmarks and metrics from plain LLMs.
  - LLM top metrics: Accuracy 20.9%, Pass Rate 16.4%, F1 11.9%, Correctness 11.9%, Exact Match 6.0%.
  - Agent top metrics: Success Rate 20.0%, Accuracy 15.7%, Pass@1 12.9%, Recall/Precision/F1 8.6% each, Efficiency 5.7%, Cost 4.3%.
  - quote: "The most frequent metric used by agents is Success Rate (20.0%), followed by Pass@1 (12.9%), Accuracy (15.7%)" (p. 44)
  - Agent studies favour HotpotQA, FEVER, ALFWorld, WebShop, SWE-bench, API-Bank. LLM studies favour Defects4J, MMLU, MBPP, BigCloneBench.
  - Agent studies mostly use GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 ("only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 models were involved" in REQ agent studies, p. 42). GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 were used in "12 out of 23" and "16 out of 23" autonomous-topic papers (p. 42).

- Reported results from the surveyed papers. The survey does not run these experiments.
  - Reflexion: HumanEval first-pass 80.1% to 91.0%, ALFWorld +22%, HotPotQA +14%. quote: "first-pass success rate on the HumanEval Python programming task increased from 80.1% to 91.0%" (p. 22)
  - SWE-agent: quote: "achieving state-of-the-art pass@1 rates on SWE-bench (12.5%) and HumanEvalFix (87.7%)" (p. 18). Setup: the agent-computer interface (ACI); this is the 2024 SOTA, now far surpassed.
  - AgentCoder: quote: "pass@1 of 77.4% compared to the previous state-of-the-art result of 69.5%" (HumanEval-ET, p. 17).
  - L2MAC: quote: "achieving a Pass@1 score of 90.2% on the HumanEval benchmark" (p. 17).
  - XUAT-Copilot (WeChat Pay UAT, 450 cases): quote: "Pass@1 rate of 88.55%, compared to 22.65% for the single-agent system and 81.96% for the variant without the reflection component" (p. 33).
  - PRIMEVUL: quote: "a state-of-the-art 7B model scored an F1 of 68.26% on BigVul but only 3.09% on PRIMEVUL" (p. 36). This shows benchmark leakage inflating scores.
  - Voting inference: more LLM calls help, then hurt. quote: "performance improves initially with more calls but declines after reaching a certain threshold" (p. 20).
  - ChatDev: quote: "design and generate software in an average of 409.84 seconds at a cost of only $0.2967" (p. 28).
  - RAG vs long context: quote: "RAG could be 99 percent cheaper than utilizing all tokens" (p. 7). No setup is given, and it is cited via Gemini 1.5 NIAH work [46].

- The survey claims agents beat LLMs on autonomy, tool use and multi-agent work. Its own analysis concedes the cost side.
  - quote: "Considering the cost, using LLMs for test generation only is enough and more cost saving than using LLM-based agents." (p. 33)
  - quote: "build a LLM-based agents framework only for the software test generation task are 'overkill'" (p. 33)
  - quote: "In terms of efficiency and cost, LLMs are still slightly superior to LLM-based agents in text generation and vulnerability detection." (p. 29)

- Single versus multi-agent framing (p. 8). Multi-agent systems are said to address single-agent limits through six points: enhanced context management, specialization and division of labor, robustness and error correction, contextual consistency, scalability and flexibility, and dynamic problem solving. These are asserted, not measured. Hallucination: "prompt engineering or tool interventions can mitigate the affect caused by hallucination, but it cannot be entirely eliminated" (p. 8).

- Auto-GPT failure modes, reported from [149] (p. 28): "task or goal skipping, generating unnecessary code or files (hallucinations), repetitive or looping responses, lack of task completion verification mechanisms."

LIMITS
Stated open challenges (Section X-D, pp. 45-46):
1. No standard agent definition or evaluation protocol. quote: "there is currently no consensus in the academic community regarding the level of autonomy, planning capability, and tool usage required for an LLM to qualify as an agent."
2. Workflow complexity and error propagation in multi-agent systems: synchronization, error recovery, context sharing, "cascading misunderstandings".
3. Tool integration bottlenecks: "fragile interfaces and poor adaptability", with no standard evaluation under tool latency, failure or partial observability.
4. Little cross-task generalization or knowledge transfer.
5. Data scarcity and too few simulation environments for multi-turn, multi-role evaluation.
6. Opaque reasoning, so low trust: "the interpretability of decision traces... remains a key obstacle to deployment."

Future directions (p. 45-46):
- A unified agent taxonomy and evaluation scale.
- Structured memory, error-trajectory analysis and goal-driven retrospection.
- Human-in-the-loop and multimodal GUI agents.
- Project-level context. quote: "Most current LLM-based Agents remain focused on function-level or module-level code completion".

My own reading of the survey's weaknesses:
- Its agent criteria are a judgement call. For example, the self-collaboration framework is classed as an agent although "it lacks external tool integration and dynamic adjustment capabilities" (p. 16). The Cycle framework is classed as an LLM application because its pipeline follows a fixed pattern.
- Counts are internally inconsistent. The text says 139 papers, Section X-A also says "a total of 110 papers", Fig. 12 sums to 153, and Fig. 1 (read from the axis text) sums to about 138.
- Some background claims are doubtful: GPT-4 at "approximately 175 billion" parameters, PaLM "up to 54 billion", and OPT as comparable in size to GPT-4. Do not cite these.
- Typos in the source: "3982 out of 2780 defects" for FixAgent on Codeflaws; MGSM is described as "Multimodal Generalized Sequence Modeling".
- The survey is SE-only and mostly descriptive. It reports results without controlling for model, budget or benchmark leakage.
- It has dated: its numbers are 2024-era (SWE-bench 12.5%, GPT-3.5/4).

BUILDS ON
- Xi et al. 2023, "The rise and potential of large language model based agents: A survey" [10]
- Wang et al., "A survey on large language model based autonomous agents" (Frontiers of CS 2024) [9]
- Fan et al. 2023, "Large language models for software engineering: Survey and open problems" [8]
- Hou et al. 2024 [17]
- Agent frameworks it draws definitions from: ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) [41], Reflexion [59], ExpeL (Zhao et al., AAAI 2024) [40], Voyager (Wang et al. 2023) [43], MetaGPT [57], AgentVerse [58], SWE-agent [53], CodeAgent [54], AutoCodeRover [55/192], GOEX [56].
- Sources on world scope: Bisk et al. 2020 "Experience grounds language" [15]. Russell and Norvig 2016 [13] and Jennings 2000 [14] are cited for historical agents.

CODE
None. The survey has no code.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p. 2): papers per year, 2020-2024, LLMs vs agents. It shows agent papers rising to 42 in 2024 (axis text; the series labelling is ambiguous in the extraction).
- Fig. 2 (p. 2) and Fig. 12 (p. 43): paper distribution across the six topics for LLMs vs agents. They show where agent research concentrates.
- Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 (pp. 12, 19): paired diagrams of an LLM-based agent versus an LLM pipeline for user-story refinement and for code generation.
- Fig. 7 (p. 24): ExpeL combined with Reflexion. Actor, evaluator and reflector feed a memory pool and an insight extractor. This is the only memory/experience-loop diagram.
- Fig. 8 (p. 33): the XUAT-Copilot agent, with perception module, inspection, operation and parameter-selection agents, and a skill library, against the Fuzz4All LLM pipeline.
- Fig. 9 (p. 39): RepairAgent (state machine, tools, dynamic prompting) against MOREPAIR (fine-tuned LLM).
- Fig. 14 (p. 45): top-10 metrics, LLM vs agent.
- Figures 10, 11 and 13 show model and benchmark usage. I did not run the captions script, so these descriptions come from the text.

PROBLEMS
- The extraction is clean, apart from tables flattened into running text, some garbled figure axis labels, and OCR-style typos ("Maintainance", "ssecurity").
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF.
- There is no explicit perception/memory/planning/action component taxonomy. Anything of that shape in the target note would have to come from Xi et al. or Wang et al., not this paper.
- The survey's source for the 99%-cheaper RAG claim has no setup stated in this text.
- Working copy of the extraction: /tmp/jin.txt. The PDF is at /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/03-agentic-foundations/sources/jin-2024-llms-llm-based-agents-software.pdf.
